title: Signature Solution - Building
summary: Students build their signature solution by following their approved plan, evaluate and flag every output, and log one evidence-based improvement as evaluate -> change -> result.
objectives: Build the solution by following the plan and prompt structure.
Evaluate outputs for accuracy and flag any that are incorrect or unclear.
Make at least one improvement based on an output check.
Keep personal and identifying data out of every prompt and keep a person in the loop for anything flagged.

body: Today you build for real. You will follow your approved plan, run your inputs, and look hard at every output - not just the ones that look right. When you find an answer that is wrong or unclear, you flag it, change one thing, and watch what happens. This is how real systems get better: one careful change, one honest result. Keep every prompt free of personal data, and keep a person in the loop for anything you flag.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can build my solution by following my approved plan.
I can evaluate outputs and flag ones that are wrong or unclear.
I can make one improvement and explain what changed and why.
I can keep personal data out of every prompt.

terms.definition: Turning your approved plan into a working solution by following it step by step.
Judging an output against your check to decide if it is correct and clear.
Marking an output that is wrong or unclear so it gets attention and a fix.
One deliberate change made in response to an evaluation.
The evaluate -> change -> result cycle that makes a solution better over time.

sections.heading: Follow the plan, do not improvise
body: Building means running your approved prompt structure on defined inputs, not inventing new prompts on the spot.
Record each output before you change anything. That way you can see what your solution really does.

sections.heading: Evaluate, flag, improve
body: Evaluate each output against your check: correct, unclear, or wrong. Flag anything that fails.
Then make one improvement and re-run. Record it as **evaluate -> change -> result** so the cause of the improvement is clear.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
body: You will build your solution from your approved plan, evaluate the outputs, flag errors, and log one improvement. The teacher runs the AI on the board; you do not log in.
items: Restate your goal and check on your log.
Run your prompt structure on defined curated inputs and record each output.
Evaluate each output and flag the wrong or unclear ones.
Make one improvement in response to a flag and re-run it.
Log the loop as evaluate -> change -> result.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: How did you tell a subtly wrong output from a correct one?
Why is one change at a time better than many at once?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the one improvement you made and why.
Write what you would evaluate more carefully next time.

worksheet.title: Week 8 - Core - Worksheet | Signature Solution - Building

questions.prompt: Maya is building her signature solution today. Put her five steps in the order the lesson says a build should follow.

items.text: Restate your goal and your check at the top of your log.
Run your approved prompt structure on the curated inputs and record every output.
Evaluate each output against your check and flag the ones that are wrong or unclear.
Make one change in response to a flag and re-run it.
Log what happened as evaluate -> change -> result.

feedback.correct: Recording every output before you change anything is what lets you prove the change caused the improvement.
feedback.incorrect: You evaluate and flag first, then change one thing: an improvement has to be a response to something you judged against your check.

questions.prompt: Sami flags one wrong output. Before re-running, he adds examples to his prompt, rewrites the instruction and swaps the input - all at once. The new output is correct. What is the problem with Sami's improvement log?

options.text: He cannot tell which of the three changes made the output correct.
He should have waited until all his inputs had been run before flagging anything.
He is not allowed to change his prompt once his plan has been approved.
An output that is correct after a change does not need to go in the log.

feedback.correct: With three changes in one re-run, the result cannot be traced to a cause, which is why the lesson asks for one change at a time.
feedback.incorrect: The output did become correct, so the problem is not the flagging or the recording - it is that three changes at once hide which one actually worked.

questions.prompt: Layla says her build followed today's rules. Which of these show she built her solution the way the lesson describes? Select all that apply.

options.text: She ran her approved prompt structure on the curated inputs she had planned.
She recorded every output before she changed anything.
She evaluated all five outputs, including the ones that looked right.
She invented a new prompt on the spot when the first output looked odd.
She used a classmate's full name as one of her test inputs.

feedback.correct: Following the approved structure, recording outputs before changing anything and checking even the outputs that look right are what make a build honest.
feedback.incorrect: Inventing a new prompt on the spot is improvising, not building to the plan, and a classmate's name is personal data that must never go into a prompt.

questions.prompt: These four lines come from one student's improvement log. Match each line to the part of the loop it is doing.

left.text: Output 3 labelled a tablet charger as 'other', which fails my check.
I marked output 3 so it would get attention and a fix.
I added a rule to my prompt listing chargers and cables as devices.
On the re-run, output 3 said 'devices' and 5 of 5 were correct.

feedback.correct: A complete loop shows the judgement, the flag it raised, the single change made in response, and the result that was actually observed.
feedback.incorrect: Judging an output against your check is evaluating; marking it so it gets attention and a fix is flagging; what you did to the prompt is the change; what happened on the re-run is the result.

questions.prompt: True or false: once you have found one output that is clearly wrong, the outputs that already look right do not need to be evaluated.

feedback.correct: Every output is judged against the check, because a subtly wrong output is the one most likely to slip through looking fine.
feedback.incorrect: Outputs that look right can still fail the check - that is why the lesson asks you to evaluate all of them, not just the obvious failures.

formative.targets: Monitors build against the plan; each student logs one evaluation-based improvement
formative.check: Build check-in against plan + one logged improvement ('evaluate -> change -> result')
formative.successCriteria: Solution follows the plan, outputs are evaluated, and one improvement is made and explained.
